subject: Dealing with zero values when using the Bootstrap Particle Filter

messages.author: 08d7d872077e52b9
messages.subject: Dealing with zero values when using the Bootstrap Particle Filter
parts:
Dear all,

I am attempting to fit an SIR-style model using particle filter MCMC. I am trying to do this in Nimble using the inbuilt bootstrap filter. Everything is building and compiling just fine, however I'm getting a lot of this warning: 
warning: logProb of data node y[1]: logProb is -Inf.

I think the problem is that my model is producing some zero simulation values, and because the likelihood function is a binomial distribution, this results in a -inf likelihood for any data point other than zero for that particular SMC step. This then forces the entire run to have a -inf likelihood. 

Could the solution be to increase the number of particles in the bootstrap filter? If so, how might I do that? Or do you think a different particle filter algorithm would be more appropriate?

I have attached my code if this helps better illustrate the problem. 

Many thanks,
Debbie

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with zero values when using the Bootstrap Particle Filter
parts:
Hi Debbie,

Thanks for the question and the reproducible example.  It's great to see this application.

I think the main issue is your state-space model formulation has z[i, 1:3] depending on z.init[1:3] for all time steps (time = i, IIUC).  My guess is that for a traditional state-space structure you will want something like this:

  z[1,1:3] <- SIB.markov.nim(z.init = z.init[1:3], theta = theta[1:4]) 
  y[1] ~ dbin(prob = p, size = z[1,2])
  for(i in 2:n) {
    z[i,1:3] <- SIB.markov.nim(z = z[i-1,1:3], theta = theta[1:4]) 
    y[i] ~ dbin(prob = p, size = z[i,2])
  }

That way, the first z[1, 1:3] depends on z.init, and later z[i, 1:3] depends on the previous values of z, i.e. z[i-1, 1:3].

A side issue is I want to make sure you are using up-to-date versions, including library(nimbleSMC), where we moved buildBoostrapFilter and the others.  Just in case you haven't seen it, here is an extensive paper in Journal of Statistical Software on the sequential Monte Carlo methods in nimbleSMC: http://statistik-jstat.uibk.ac.at/article/view/v100i03

I was able to run this version and get a numeric answer (using smaller choices of m (number of particles) and n (length of series) for testing because with m=1000 and n=80 it is pretty slow).

Note that it is possible to arrange initial states in different ways and I'm not sure if I've done exactly what you want.

I hope that gets you going!

Perry

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with zero values when using the Bootstrap Particle Filter
parts:
Hi Debbie,

I realized another issue going on here.  The latent states need to have a stochastic declaration.  This means your SIB.markov needs to be provided as a distribution, rather than a function.  That allows nimbleModel to make sense of the graphical model relationships correctly and allows buildBootstrapFilter to figure out what needs to be done at each step.  A reason it was running so slowly is that "z[i, 1:3] <- SIB.markov(...)" was declared as deterministic, so that the entire time sequence was viewed as deterministic rather than stochastic.  Here is what I think you need to do:

# This is a dummy "d" function that just returns 0. 
# For SMC, you only need to draw from SIB.markov, not calculate probabilities, so this is just a placeholder to keep nimble happy.
# The arguments are as required for a user-defined distribution: x is first, log is last
dSIB.markov <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1), z.init = double(1), theta = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
  return(0) # dummy value
  returnType(double())
})

# rename SIB.markov to rSIB.markov.R
# and add an n argument that can be ignored but is required for a user-defined "r" function.
rSIB.markov.R <- function(n, z.init, theta){
... <contents of your SIB.markov>
}

# rename to rSIB.markov to match dSIB.markov.  These names must match except for the "r" and the "d".
# This is what nimble will use as the user-defined "r" function for dSIB.markov
rSIB.markov <- nimbleRcall(function(n = integer(0), z.init = double(1), theta = double(1)){}, Rfun = 'rSIB.markov.R', returnType = double(1))

# Change model code to:
z[1,1:3] ~ dSIB.markov(z.init = z.init[1:3], theta = theta[1:4]) # will call rSIB.markov for stochastic draws

y[1] ~ dbin(prob = p, size = z[1,2])
  for(i in 2:n){
z[i,1:3] ~ dSIB.markov(z = z[i-1,1:3], theta = theta[1:4]) # ditto

y[i] ~ dbin(prob = p, size = z[i,2])
  }

Now nimble and nimbleSMC know that each z[i, 1:3] is a stochastic node, and it should decompose the model structure correctly.

Phew, I hope that works!

Perry
